claims.text: An anemic domain model has classes named after business things, such as Order, whose data any code can change, while every rule about that data lives in other classes.
claims.source_hint: glossary anemic-domain-model; .NET microservices guide: Design a microservice domain model (anemic domain model)

claims.text: At stage-1 Order has a public getter and a public setter for every property (Id, CustomerId, PlacedAt, Status, Items, Customer) and no methods.
The comment at the top of Entities.cs at stage-1 says: 'One class per table in db/schema.sql. No behaviour here beyond what a row is.'

Status has a public setter, so any class holding an Order can assign any string and the compiler accepts it (also against OrderExposed's public field); the orders CHECK in db/schema.sql accepts any of new/paid/shipped/cancelled, whatever the current one.
claims.source_hint: C# docs: Properties; examples/don-hang @ stage-1: Entities.cs:30, OrderExposed.cs:9, db/schema.sql:22-23

claims.text: The `required` modifier on Status only forces code that creates an Order (object initializer) to set Status; it does not restrict which value is set or later assignments.

At stage-1 the only rule about orders in the C# code is the empty-items check in PlaceOrderAsync; no code checks which status may follow which, and CancelOrderAsync sets Status to cancelled on any order it finds, including a shipped one.
OrderDto (DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs) is a record the API uses to answer clients, holding data and no rules; the file's comment says the API answers in these shapes, never in the entity shapes.
A DTO carries data across a boundary and is meant to have no rules; an anemic domain model stands for a business thing that has rules yet holds none of them.
claims.source_hint: outline item 5; .NET microservices guide: anemic domain model vs DTO

claims.text: An anemic domain model is a reasonable choice when the data has no rules that scripts must check (Product at stage-1: its one business rule, price above zero, is a database CHECK); it becomes a cost once rules appear and get repeated across scripts.
claims.source_hint: outline item 6; .NET microservices guide: 'anemic domain model ... might be good enough' for simple CRUD

claims.text: OrderExposed (samples, stage-1) has public fields Id, Status, TotalVnd, Lines, and its comment says any code anywhere can put an order into a state the business does not allow.

At stage-1, git grep -n "Status = \"" -- "DonHang.*/*.cs" prints three lines: OrderService.cs:16 (Status = "new"), OrderService.cs:34 (order.Status = "cancelled"), OrderServiceTests.cs:49 (Status = "new" in a seeded test order).
claims.source_hint: verified: git grep -n 'Status = "' stage-1 -- "DonHang.*/*.cs" in examples/don-hang

claims.text: At stage-1 Product has only Id, Name and PriceVnd with public setters, and no C# code checks their values; its one business rule, a price above zero, is a CHECK in db/schema.sql.
Being mapped to a table does not by itself make a class anemic: a mapped class could still hold rules in methods; what makes Order anemic is that its rules live in other classes.
